data.title: Vesicobullous diseases (pemphigus / pemphigoid) — viva
data.summary: Vesicobullous diseases · 20 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Vesicobullous diseases (pemphigus / pemphigoid)** (Vesicobullous diseases)_

**Q1. Classify vesiculobullous disorders (PYQ).**
- Genetic: epidermolysis bullosa (simplex, junctional, dystrophic, Kindler), Hailey–Hailey, Darier's (rarely bullous), bullous ichthyosiform erythroderma, porphyrias
- Autoimmune intraepidermal: pemphigus vulgaris, foliaceus (endemic fogo selvagem, pemphigus erythematosus/Senear–Usher), IgA pemphigus, paraneoplastic pemphigus, drug-induced pemphigus, pemphigus vegetans, herpetiformis
- Autoimmune subepidermal: bullous pemphigoid, mucous membrane pemphigoid, pemphigoid gestationis, linear IgA bullous dermatosis/chronic bullous disease of childhood, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, dermatitis herpetiformis, bullous SLE, anti-p200 (anti-laminin γ1) pemphigoid
- Infections (bullous impetigo, SSSS, herpes, varicella), drug (SJS/TEN, FDE), physical (burns, friction, cold, insect bites), metabolic (diabetic bullae, porphyria), others (bullous LP, bullous mastocytosis)

**Q2. Explain the pathogenesis of pemphigus (desmoglein compensation theory).**
- IgG (mainly IgG4) autoantibodies against desmogleins (desmosomal cadherins) → loss of keratinocyte adhesion (acantholysis) via steric hindrance and signalling (p38 MAPK)
- Dsg1 expressed mostly in superficial epidermis, Dsg3 in deep epidermis and mucosa (where Dsg1 is scant)
- Mucosal-dominant PV: anti-Dsg3 only (mucosa fails, skin protected by Dsg1); mucocutaneous PV: anti-Dsg3 + anti-Dsg1 (suprabasal split in skin and mucosa); PF: anti-Dsg1 only (subcorneal split in skin; mucosa protected by Dsg3)
- Same theory explains bullous impetigo/SSSS (exfoliative toxin cleaves Dsg1)
- Genetic: HLA-DRB1*04:02, DQB1*05:03; triggers — drugs (thiol drugs like penicillamine, captopril), UV, burns, pregnancy, stress, diet (garlic, thiols)

**Q3. Clinical features of pemphigus vulgaris.**
- Age 40–60; oral erosions first in ~70% (buccal mucosa, palate, gingiva) — may precede skin by months; painful, slow-healing
- Flaccid blisters on normal skin of scalp, face, axillae, groin, trunk → rupture to painful erosions that bleed and enlarge; heal without scars (hyperpigmentation)
- Nikolsky sign and bulla spread (Asboe-Hansen) positive
- Other mucosae: conjunctiva, nose, larynx (hoarseness), pharynx, oesophagus, genitals, anus; nails — paronychia, haemorrhages

**Q4. Clinical features of pemphigus foliaceus.**
- Superficial flaccid blisters rarely seen; scaly crusted erosions with 'cornflake' scales in seborrhoeic distribution (face, scalp, upper trunk); no mucosal involvement; may become erythrodermic
- Pemphigus erythematosus (Senear–Usher): localised PF of malar area with lupus serology/ DIF overlap
- Endemic PF (fogo selvagem — Brazil) linked to black fly bites
- Drug-induced: thiol drugs more often PF pattern

**Q5. What is paraneoplastic pemphigus?**
- Associated with lymphoproliferative neoplasms (non-Hodgkin lymphoma, CLL, Castleman disease, thymoma)
- Severe intractable stomatitis (lips, tongue), polymorphic skin lesions (PV-like, BP-like, EM-like, lichenoid, GVHD-like), conjunctivitis; bronchiolitis obliterans (often fatal)
- Antibodies to plakins (envoplakin, periplakin, desmoplakin), Dsg3, A2ML1; IIF on rat bladder epithelium positive
- Poor prognosis; treat tumour, rituximab, IVIG

**Q6. Tzanck smear in pemphigus.**
- Scraping from base of a fresh bulla stained with Giemsa: acantholytic cells — rounded keratinocytes with large hyperchromatic nuclei, perinuclear halo and condensed peripheral cytoplasm ('fried-egg' appearance) — screening test only; also seen in SSSS, Hailey–Hailey, Darier's, herpes

**Q7. Describe the role of immunofluorescence (PYQ).**
- DIF (perilesional skin in Michel's medium) — gold standard: pemphigus — intercellular IgG/C3 in fish-net/chicken-wire pattern (PF more upper epidermis); BP — linear IgG/C3 along BMZ; DH — granular IgA in dermal papillae; LABD — linear IgA; lupus — granular IgG/IgM/C3 at BMZ (lupus band)
- IIF (patient serum): pemphigus on monkey oesophagus (PV) or guinea-pig oesophagus (PF) — titre correlates with activity; salt-split skin — roof binding (BP, LABD) vs floor binding (EBA, anti-laminin 332 MMP, anti-p200, bullous SLE)
- ELISA: anti-Dsg1, Dsg3 (indices track disease activity, guide stopping therapy), BP180 (NC16A), BP230, collagen VII; BIOCHIP multiplex

**Q8. Histopathology of PV, PF and BP.**
- PV: suprabasal cleft with acantholysis, basal cells attached to the floor like a 'row of tombstones', eosinophilic spongiosis early
- PF: subcorneal/granular layer split with acantholysis
- BP: subepidermal blister with eosinophils (cell-rich), eosinophilic spongiosis in urticarial phase; cell-poor in some

**Q9. Write a short note on Nikolsky sign (PYQ).**
- Dislodgement of the epidermis by lateral pressure on apparently normal skin — indicates intraepidermal loss of cohesion
- Positive: pemphigus (PV, PF), SSSS, TEN (on erythematous skin), EB (some), bullous impetigo; negative in BP, DH, EBA
- Variants: marginal Nikolsky (extension of blister edge), direct (on normal skin away from lesions), Asboe-Hansen (bulla-spread) sign, Sheklakov's sign

**Q10. Clinical features of bullous pemphigoid (BP).**
- Commonest autoimmune blistering disease; elderly (>70); IgG against BP180 (collagen XVII, NC16A domain) and BP230 in hemidesmosomes
- Prodromal (non-bullous) phase: itchy urticarial or eczematous plaques for weeks–months
- Tense, large, clear or haemorrhagic blisters on normal or erythematous skin of flexures, lower abdomen, thighs; heal without scars (milia occasionally); mucosa involved in 10–30% (mild)
- Associations: neurological disease (dementia, Parkinson's, stroke), drugs (DPP-4 inhibitors — gliptins, especially vildagliptin; loop diuretics, spironolactone, PD-1 inhibitors), psoriasis (and its phototherapy)

**Q11. Differentiate pemphigus vulgaris from bullous pemphigoid.**
- PV: middle age, mucosa almost always, flaccid fragile blisters, erosions predominate, Nikolsky +, suprabasal acantholysis, intercellular IgG on DIF, anti-Dsg3/1, more severe, needs immunosuppression
- BP: elderly, mucosa rarely, tense intact blisters, intense itch, Nikolsky –, subepidermal blister with eosinophils, linear IgG/C3 at BMZ, anti-BP180/230, can respond to topical steroids

**Q12. Management of pemphigus.**
- General: admit severe disease; barrier nursing, fluid–electrolyte, nutrition, wound care (non-adherent dressings, saline/potassium permanganate soaks), pain control, oral care (steroid mouthwash, lignocaine), treat infections, eye/ENT care
- Severity: PDAI (Pemphigus Disease Area Index) or ABSIS
- First line: systemic prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day with steroid-sparing adjuvant (azathioprine 2–2.5 mg/kg after TPMT check, or mycophenolate mofetil 2–3 g/day) — as in our treatment ladder
- Rituximab (anti-CD20) — highly effective: rheumatoid arthritis protocol 1 g IV on day 1 and day 15 (or lymphoma protocol 375 mg/m² weekly × 4), with short steroid; maintenance 500 mg at 6 months/relapse — international guidelines now place it first-line for moderate–severe PV (Ritux 3 trial)
- Other options: dexamethasone–cyclophosphamide pulse (DCP — Pasricha; Indian regimen), IVIG 2 g/kg/cycle monthly (useful in infections/refractory/pregnancy), cyclophosphamide, plasmapheresis/immunoadsorption, dapsone (PF), methotrexate, newer: BTK inhibitors, FcRn blockers (efgartigimod) under study
- Prophylaxis while on steroids: calcium + vitamin D, bisphosphonate, PPI, deworming (ivermectin/albendazole — strongyloides), TB screening, blood sugar/BP monitoring, PCP prophylaxis with rituximab in some, HBV screening before rituximab

**Q13. Discuss pulse therapy (PYQ).**
- Administration of supra-pharmacological doses of drugs intermittently to achieve faster response and reduce long-term side effects
- Dexamethasone–cyclophosphamide pulse (DCP, Pasricha 1984): dexamethasone 100 mg in 500 ml 5% dextrose IV over 2 h on 3 consecutive days + cyclophosphamide 500 mg IV on day 1, repeated every 4 weeks; plus oral cyclophosphamide 50 mg daily between pulses
- Phases: I — pulses + daily cyclophosphamide until complete remission; II — continue pulses for 9 months; III — oral cyclophosphamide 50 mg daily for 9 months; IV — no treatment (follow-up)
- Side effects: hyperglycaemia, hypertension, arrhythmia, electrolyte disturbance, infections; cyclophosphamide — haemorrhagic cystitis (mesna, hydration), infertility/amenorrhoea, bone marrow suppression, malignancy
- Other pulses: methylprednisolone pulse 1 g × 3 days, dexamethasone–azathioprine pulse, oral mini-pulse (OMP) for vitiligo/LP

**Q14. Comment on the role of diet in pemphigus (PYQ).**
- Thiol-containing foods (garlic, onion, leek, chives) and phenol/tannin-rich foods (tea, betel nut, mango, cassava) and isothiocyanates (mustard) reported to trigger acantholysis in susceptible persons — advise moderation
- Practical: soft bland high-protein diet for oral lesions, avoid spicy/hard foods; diabetic and low-salt diet while on steroids; adequate calcium and vitamin D

**Q15. Management of bullous pemphigoid.**
- Localised/mild: super-potent topical clobetasol propionate 0.05% (whole body 30–40 g/day in extensive disease — as effective as oral steroids with fewer deaths, French trial)
- Doxycycline 200 mg/day ± nicotinamide (BLISTER trial — non-inferior, safer than prednisolone in elderly)
- Moderate–severe: prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day with taper; adjuvants — methotrexate (low dose, elderly), azathioprine, mycophenolate, dapsone
- Refractory: rituximab, IVIG, omalizumab, dupilumab (approved for BP in some countries — confirm), stop culprit drug (gliptin)
- Care: skin — drain tense blisters with sterile needle leaving roof, wound care; monitor steroid complications in elderly

**Q16. Discuss differential diagnosis of bullae in children (PYQ).**
- Infective: bullous impetigo, SSSS, varicella, HSV, hand-foot-mouth disease
- Genetic: epidermolysis bullosa, incontinentia pigmenti (vesicular stage), bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, Hailey–Hailey (adolescents), bullous mastocytosis, porphyria (CEP, EPP)
- Immune: chronic bullous disease of childhood (linear IgA — 'string of pearls'/cluster of jewels around genitals and face), childhood BP, juvenile PV (rare), DH, bullous SLE
- Others: insect bite bullae, burns/scalds (child abuse), friction blisters, fixed drug eruption, SJS/TEN, Kawasaki (desquamation), phytophotodermatitis

**Q17. Write short notes on pemphigoid gestationis (PYQ).**
- Rare autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease of pregnancy (2nd–3rd trimester) or puerperium; IgG1 against BP180 (complement-fixing); HLA-DR3/DR4 association; linked to molar pregnancy and choriocarcinoma
- Itchy urticarial papules/plaques starting around the umbilicus then tense blisters spreading to trunk and limbs (face, mucosa spared); flares at delivery; recurs in subsequent pregnancies (earlier and more severe) and with OCP
- DIF: linear C3 (± IgG) at BMZ — distinguishes from polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (DIF negative, starts in striae, spares umbilicus)
- Fetal: small-for-gestational-age, prematurity, transient neonatal blisters (passive antibodies)
- Treatment: potent topical steroids, oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day; antihistamines; IVIG/cyclosporine for refractory

**Q18. Name the dermatoses of pregnancy.**
- Pemphigoid gestationis, polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP/PUPPP), intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (itch without primary lesions, raised bile acids — fetal risk, ursodeoxycholic acid), atopic eruption of pregnancy (commonest — eczema/prurigo, early onset)

**Q19. What is dermatitis herpetiformis?**
- Cutaneous manifestation of gluten-sensitive enteropathy (coeliac disease); IgA against epidermal transglutaminase (TG3)
- Intensely itchy grouped papulovesicles/excoriations on extensors (elbows, knees, buttocks, scalp, shoulders), symmetrical
- Histology: neutrophilic microabscesses in dermal papillae; DIF: granular IgA in dermal papillae (diagnostic)
- Treatment: strict lifelong gluten-free diet (reduces lymphoma risk), dapsone (rapid itch relief — check G6PD), sulfapyridine

**Q20. Prognosis and remission definitions in pemphigus.**
- Mortality fell from ~75% pre-steroid era to <5–10% now (mostly infections and steroid complications)
- Complete remission off therapy: no new lesions for ≥2 months off all systemic therapy; complete remission on minimal therapy: prednisolone ≤10 mg/day (and/or minimal adjuvant) for ≥2 months; relapse: ≥3 new lesions/month not healing in 1 week (consensus definitions)

## Quick spotter facts
- Row of tombstones — PV
- Fish-net intercellular IgG — pemphigus; linear IgG/C3 BMZ — BP; granular IgA in papillae — DH
- Dsg compensation: Dsg3 only = mucosal PV; Dsg1 only = PF

## Note
Our treatment ladder: 1st line steroid + azathioprine; 2nd rituximab/MMF; 3rd DCP/IVIG (her decision). Rituximab first-line in international guidelines is mentioned for viva awareness.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Autoimmune vesiculobullous disorders); Indian consensus on pemphigus (IADVL/ IJDVL) and rituximab use. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
